opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I look back, it doesn't feel like a carefully planned path. It feels more like a series of small accidents that slowly started to make sense.

As an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, I was in a very engineering-heavy, competition-oriented environment. I liked programming and math, but I didn't have a clear picture of what "research" really meant. Vision was attractive partly for a very simple reason: you can *see* the results. You train something and look at the output, and you immediately get a feeling for whether it's working. That kind of direct feedback was very appealing to me.

Then I went to UC San Diego for my PhD and worked with Zhuowen Tu. That period overlapped with the deep learning wave really taking off, around 2012 to 2014. It was a strange and exciting time, because a lot of what we had learned in classical computer vision was suddenly being questioned. Projects like edge detection, HED for example, were a way for me to learn how to think about representations, about how networks see structure, not just how to push a benchmark number.

After that I went to FAIR, and that was another big shift. Being around people like Kaiming and Ross, I learned a kind of taste: simple ideas that actually work, very careful experiments, and being honest about what's really contributing to the result. ResNeXt and later ConvNeXt came out of that mindset. ConvNeXt in particular was almost a question rather than a method: do we really understand why Transformers are winning, or are we confusing architecture with training recipes?

So if I try to make sense of it, I'd say my path has been driven less by a single topic and more by a recurring curiosity: *what is the right representation of the visual world, and how do we learn it?* Recognition, architectures, self-supervised learning, generative models like diffusion transformers, and now multimodal and world-model-style work: to me they're all different angles on the same question.

And I think vision is at a really interesting moment right now. Language models have gotten so strong that some people think vision is just another input modality to plug into an LLM. I don't fully believe that. Seeing, understanding space, physics, interacting with the world, that's a deeper kind of intelligence, and I feel computer vision still has a lot to say about it. That's probably what keeps me in this field.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes what keeps them in computer vision but does not urge researchers to see their contribution as something that would not happen without them.

r002.rationale: The candidate links their research path and work—including HED, ResNeXt, and ConvNeXt—to personal academic experiences, the timing of deep learning’s rise, and lessons learned at FAIR.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I look back it feels less like a plan and more like a series of lucky accidents that I only later learned to connect.

I grew up in China and did my undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. At the time I wasn't a "vision person" at all. I was just someone who liked math and liked building things, and computer science felt like the place where those two could coexist. Vision came in almost sideways. I remember being fascinated by this very simple question: how does a machine actually see? You give it a grid of numbers, and somehow out of that it's supposed to understand a cat, a street, a face. That gap between pixels and meaning felt almost philosophical to me, and I think that's what pulled me in.

Then I went to UC San Diego for my PhD and worked with Zhuowen Tu. That was the period when deep learning was going from a niche thing that a few people believed in to the thing everyone suddenly had to care about. I was lucky to be in the room when that transition happened. My early work was on things like edge detection, which sounds very unglamorous, but it taught me to think about structure, about how low-level signals compose into higher-level representations. A lot of what I did later, including the work on ResNeXt and the ideas about network design, came out of that habit of thinking in terms of building blocks and how they aggregate.

After that I spent time at Facebook AI Research, and that environment really shaped me. You're surrounded by people who are both deeply rigorous and extremely pragmatic. I learned that good research isn't just about having a clever idea, it's about asking a clean question, running the experiment carefully, and being honest about what the result actually tells you. Things like the ConvNeXt work came from that spirit: not "let's invent something new," but "let's really understand what's driving progress, and separate the architecture from the training recipe."

And now I'm at NYU, teaching and running a group, and that's changed how I think again. Students ask you why, constantly, and you realize how many things you believed just because the field believed them. So I've become more interested in the fundamentals, in representation learning, in whether our models actually understand the visual world or just do very good pattern matching, and in how vision connects to language and other modalities.

So if I try to make sense of it, I'd say the thread is curiosity about perception, a taste for simplicity, and a bit of stubbornness about understanding why things work rather than just that they work. The rest was timing and good mentors. I try to remind myself of that whenever I'm tempted to take too much credit for the path.

r001.rationale: The response credits timing and mentors and describes a personal research path, but it does not urge researchers to view their contributions as things that would never happen without them.

r002.rationale: The response connects the researcher’s path through university, doctoral work, and research environments to later outcomes, including ResNeXt and ConvNeXt.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think it’s less of a straight line than it might appear. You get interested in a question, you start working on it, and that experience changes what you want to understand next.

For me, computer vision brings together two things: the very intuitive question of how we make sense of what we see, and the technical question of how a machine can learn to do that. You can build something and test it, but the results also push you to rethink your assumptions. That back-and-forth is what makes the research interesting to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes research as an iterative process but does not urge researchers to see their contribution as something only they could make.

r002.rationale: It mentions interests and research experiences shaping what comes next, but does not attribute an individual's route to a research outcome to their personal life history.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think of it less as a straight line and more as a process of discovering what kinds of questions I wanted to spend time on. Computer vision brings together two things I find compelling: understanding the visual world and building systems that can learn from it.

And there’s this constant tension between intuition and experiments. You can have a very elegant idea, but then you have to see whether it actually works—and understand why. That back-and-forth is a big part of what makes research interesting to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses curiosity and experimentation but does not say a researcher’s contribution would never happen without that researcher.
